frames.narration: The laptop starts the VPN on office Wi-Fi. It asks the directory for gateways. The directory returns three, with their current load, and the policy: send only company routes 10.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16 through the tunnel.

The laptop sends a probe to each gateway at once. Gateway A answers in 12 ms with 40% load and gateway B in 48 ms with 20% load. Cost is round trip plus a load penalty, so A scores 12 + 24 = 36 and B scores 48 + 12 = 60. A wins.

One handshake round trip. The laptop sends its ephemeral key and proof of its enrolled identity. The gateway checks it with the identity service, answers with its own ephemeral key, and both derive the same session keys. They are never sent, and a stolen long-term key would not reveal this session.

The tunnel is up after one round trip, about 12 ms. A request for 10.4.1.9 matches 10.0.0.0/8, so it goes through the tunnel to the private app. A request to a public website does not match, and leaves directly from the laptop.

While idle, the laptop sends a tiny keepalive every 25 seconds. The home router and carrier NAT would forget the mapping after 30 to 60 seconds without traffic, so the keepalive holds it open and the gateway can still send to the laptop.

The user leaves the office and the laptop joins a mobile hotspot. It now has the address 198.51.100.7. Its next packet has the same session id 7 and a counter of 412, which is higher than any before. The gateway checks the tag and the counter, accepts it and replies to the new address. There is no new handshake.
An attacker sends a copy of the old packet with counter 412 from another address. The tag is right but the counter is not higher than 412, so the gateway discards it and does not move the session.

Load reports show that the fleet is at 75% load at the evening peak and the autoscaler wants to replace gateway A with a new version. It marks A as draining. The directory stops offering A, and A tells its devices to move.

After a random delay of 0 to 5 seconds, the laptop presents its resumption ticket to gateway B. B decrypts it, finds the same session key and counter, and continues without a login. Applications keep their TCP connections. When A has no sessions left, it shuts down.
